Request to
approve the contract extension for the Courier Service for
Lancashire School Libraries.
 
A courier
service has been contracted by the Lancashire School Library
Service (SLS) to facilitate the collection and distribution of
books, learning resources and other materials between the service
depot and subscribing schools across Lancashire. SLS operates as a
traded service within Lancashire County Council's Cultural Services
and relies on an efficient and reliable courier network to support
the delivery of its services to schools.
 
The volume of
deliveries varies throughout the academic year depending on school
activity and subscription levels. On average, more than 3,000 items
are delivered annually to over 250 school locations across the
county. The courier service plays a critical role in ensuring that
educational resources are delivered and returned within agreed
timescales, enabling schools to access materials when required and
supporting continuity of service for educational
establishments.
 
The current
agreement was procured through an open tender process and commenced
on 1 December 2023. The contract was awarded for an initial term of
three years, with the option to extend for up to a further 24
months.

development.

of Delegation to Heads of Service.

purpose:
These proposals form part of the Levelling Up East Lancashire
project. They aim to deliver improvements in town centre locations
through:

• Making it safer and easier to walk and wheel around town
centres with better crossing facilities and wider pavements.
• Improving street environments and public spaces with new
paving and surfaces, planting and seating.
• Refreshing and modernising town centre spaces to support
local businesses.
• Improving routes and crossings to make it easier and safer
for people.

The proposals will work together to create a safer environment for
pedestrians, cyclists, and vulnerable users, whilst also improving
public realm in the area. The intention of the scheme is twofold,
to:

• Increase footfall in town centres and local neighbourhoods
to support business growth and investment
• Increase active travel uptake to improve health and
wellbeing and reduce health inequalities.

These proposals include the following:

• Crossing points for pedestrians to facilitate their safe
crossing of the road and minimise conflict with motor
vehicles.
• No Left Turn restriction to allow facilitate safe crossing
of pedestrians at Nelson Square junction
• Road humps, raised pedestrian crossing points and raised
junction tables to reduce vehicle speeds and improve road safety
particularly for pedestrians and vulnerable road users.
• Limited waiting restrictions to provide loading and parking
opportunities for local businesses and will help prevent vehicles
from being parked for extended periods in a high demand area.
• Providing additional blue badge holder parking and
provisions for taxis
• No Waiting at Any Time to prevent obstructive parking,
maintain clear visibility at junctions and ensure safe and
efficient movement of vehicles, cyclists and pedestrians.
• No Loading at Any Time to prevent obstruction caused by
loading activity, maintain clear sightlines and access, and enhance
safety and traffic flow.
• Minor alterations to existing No Waiting at Any Time
restrictions to facilitate the proposed changes to the road
layout.
Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 12 June 2026 and 10
July 2026 which included advertising in the local press and notices
being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.


Following formal consultation No Objections were received.

These proposals include the following:

• Crossing points for pedestrians to facilitate their safe
crossing of the road and minimise conflict with motor
vehicles.
• No Left Turn restriction to allow facilitate safe crossing
of pedestrians at Nelson Square junction
• Road humps, raised pedestrian crossing points and raised
junction tables to reduce vehicle speeds and improve road safety
particularly for pedestrians and vulnerable road users.
• Limited waiting restrictions to provide loading and parking
opportunities for local businesses and will help prevent vehicles
from being parked for extended periods in a high demand area.
• Providing additional blue badge holder parking and
provisions for taxis
• No Waiting at Any Time to prevent obstructive parking,
maintain clear visibility at junctions and ensure safe and
efficient movement of vehicles, cyclists and pedestrians.
• No Loading at Any Time to prevent obstruction caused by
loading activity, maintain clear sightlines and access, and enhance
safety and traffic flow.
• Minor alterations to existing No Waiting at Any Time
restrictions to facilitate the proposed changes to the road
layout.
Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 12 June 2026 and 10
July 2026 which included advertising in the local press and notices
being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.


Following formal consultation No Objections were received.

content:
Notice of Motion
1
 
It was moved by County
Councillor Azhar Ali OBE and seconded by County Councillor Gina
Dowding that:
 
"This council notes with
serious concern that “corridor care” – where
patients are treated in inappropriate spaces such as corridors or
waiting areas – represents a serious and worsening failure of
the health care system. No resident should be treated this
way.

Hospitals serving Lancashire residents, including Royal Preston,
Chorley and South Ribble, Blackpool Victoria, Royal Lancaster
Infirmary, and Royal Blackburn, report - on too many occasions -
severe overcrowding, long A&E waits, and unsafe
conditions.

Corridor care is undignified, unsafe, and unacceptable, placing
vulnerable patients at risk and forcing NHS staff to work under
intolerable pressure.

This Council believes corridor
care affecting Lancashire hospitals is part of a wider national
scandal, driven by insufficient capacity, workforce shortages, and
sustained pressure on NHS services.

This council resolves
to:
 

Condemn corridor care
and ask for its urgent elimination.

 

Through the
Lancashire Health and Wellbeing Board and by November 2026, work

Pickup that:
 
"This Council notes:
 

The importance of the
green belt in preserving openness and protecting Lancashire's
beautiful countryside; the unique character of its rural areas,
villages and towns; important wildlife, including red-listed
species; and the county’s ecological network identified
within the Lancashire Local Nature Recovery Strategy.

 

That planning
authorities in Lancashire have recently refused large-scale
development proposals on green belt land due to harm to openness,
landscape, identity, and ecology.

 

That Government
encouragement to reclassify some green belt land as “grey
belt” increases pressure for development in protected
areas.

 

That large housing
schemes on green belt land typically represent major urban
extensions that would permanently destroy countryside.


This Council
believes:
 

That Lancashire's
countryside and green belt is a major asset, valued by
communities.
That inappropriate
development on green belt land causes irreversible harm to
landscape character, local ecology, and rural identity.
That democratic
planning decisions must be respected, and national reinterpretation
of policy should not override well-founded refusals.


This Council
resolves:
 

To reaffirm its
commitment to our rural communities, villages and towns and to the
protection of Lancashire's green belt and countryside.

 

To ask the Chief
Executive to write to Lancashire's district councils to support
their efforts to protect green belt land in line with their local
development plan policies.

 

To ask the Chief
Executive to write to the Planning Inspectorate to affirm our
commitment to the green belt and our support for the decisions of
planning authorities and residents' views."

Use of an alternative access from Chequer Lane
for restoration vehicles and construction of a ramped access into
Ravenhead Quarry, Chequer Lane, Up Holland, WN8 0DD
content:
A report was presented on an application for
the use of an alternative access from Chequer Lane
for restoration vehicles and the construction of a ramped access
into Ravenhead Quarry, Chequer Lane, Up
Holland.
 
The report included the views
of the Health and Safety Executive, LCC Highways Development
Control, Lead Local Flood Authority, the Environment Agency, Coal
Authority, LCC Ecology Service and Natural England. One letter of
objection to the application had been received, the details of
which were set out in the Committee report.
 
No comments had been received
from West Lancashire Borough Council, Upholland Parish Council or
County Councillor Nigel Swales.
 
The Senior Planning Officer
presented a Powerpoint presentation
(which also covered the LCC/2025/0023 application for the
Ravenhead Quarry site to be considered
later on the agenda) showing a site location plan, aerial view of
the site, access proposal plan, variation of condition
restoration/infill, new access point and the boundary of the Site
of Special Scientific Interest. Also shown were photographs of the
current access off Chequer Lane and the proposed access looking
north and south along Chequer Lane and the view within the proposed
access point to the former brickworks building.
 
A representation was made
by Alistair Hoyle, agent for the applicant. A summary of the
representation is as follows: the representation can be viewed in
full at the webcast link 
here
 

Together, the applications seek to
relocate the restoration access to the former brickwork southern
entrance and make the associated amendments to the existing
planning permission.
The proposals do not increase the
approved number of HGV movements, extend the duration of the
restoration works, or alter the approved restoration strategy.
The application had been amended
since the Committee report had been written to state that no
additional construction material would be imported to construct the
access ramp.
The revised access provided improved
geometry, a dedicated wheel wash, pedestrian priority measures of
the former access, and conditions requiring all restoration traffic
to use the new access once it becomes operational.
The residential amenity will remain
acceptable.
The noise technical note confirmed
that traffic using the relocated access was unlikely to be
distinguishable from the existing rural traffic environment.
These applications deliver practical
improvements to an already approved restoration scheme without
increasing its scale or environmental impacts.

 
The officer answered questions
from Committee.
 
It was confirmed to Committee
that conditions would be attached to the planning permission
improving the facility with a new wheel wash and improved drainage.
In addition, HGV traffic entering the site would be required to
take a left turn into the site and a right turn out to access the
major road network when leaving the site. Highway safety signage
would also be put in place to reflect this.
 
Resolved:
That planning permission be granted, subject
to the conditions detailed in Appendix 'A'.

for all road users, including pedestrians.

frontagers to the proposed location of the Bus Stop being notified
and notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors
were consulted along with the council's usual consultees.
 
Following formal consultation No Objections
were received.

purpose:
As part of a countywide administrative process, we are revoking
historic 30mph "Restricted Road" Speed Limit Orders (SLOs). These
roads already carry a default 30mph speed limit under national
legislation and do not require a separate SLO.

Purpose of Revocation: This revocation is a procedural step to
remove outdated Speed Limit Orders (SLOs) and restore the roads to
their correct legal status as "restricted roads" under Section 82
of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984. It does not change the
actual speed limit or affect existing signage.

Maintaining obsolete Orders can create legal ambiguity and
enforcement challenges. This revocation ensures consistency and
clarity across Lancashire by clearly distinguishing between roads
governed by default 30mph restrictions and those with imposed 30mph
limits.

Background of Legislation: Under the Road Traffic Regulation Act
1984, a 30mph speed limit can apply in two ways:

• 30mph Speed Limit – imposed via a Speed Limit Order
(SLO), typically used where street lighting is absent or
insufficient.
• 30mph Restricted Road – a default limit that applies
automatically to roads with a system of street lighting (lamps no
more than 200 yards apart), without the need for a Speed Limit
Order to be made.

The main distinction between the two is a 30mph speed limit is an
imposed limit, whereas a 30mph restricted road is a default limit
that automatically applies due to street lighting.

If a different speed limit other than 30 mph is required on a
restricted road, a Speed Limit Order (SLO) must be introduced to
override the default.

Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 07/05/2026 until
04/06/2026 which included advertising in the local press and
notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.


Following formal consultation two responses was received. The main
points raised in the responses along with Officer comments are
outlines in Appendix C.

purpose:
This report summarises the 2025/26 outturn
position across the Council’s Revenue, Capital and Schools
Budgets. The financial position should be considered alongside
delivery of the Council Plan and associated key performance
indicators.
 
The final revenue outturn for 2025/26 is an
overspend of £2.992m, representing 0.24% of the net revenue
budget. This reflects a continued improvement throughout the year.
A significant pressure of £27.863m (2.24%) was identified at
Quarter 1, which reduced to £10.354m (0.83%) at Quarter 2 and
£6.117m (0.49%) at Quarter 3.
 
Over the course of the financial year, the
Council has maintained a clear focus on financial stability despite
a challenging operating environment, characterised by rising demand
and cost pressures. The implementation of efficiency measures and
robust in-year mitigations, supported by strong service-level
controls and corporate oversight, has culminated in the improved
outturn position.
 
The Council’s reserve position remains
robust, with the Transitional Reserve providing resilience. Reserve
utilisation is closely monitored and ensures that resources are
aligned to corporate priorities, underpinned by strong governance
arrangements. Further details of major spending variations to
budget and the resultant impact on reserves are shown in Appendix
'A'. 
 
The in-year Capital Delivery Programme was
£306.005m (after approved additions and re-profiling). The
outturn position for 2025/26 is spend of £193.229m, a
variance of -£112.776m (-36.9%). The variance is primarily
the product of delayed delivery on some schemes, arising notably
from resource, procurement and contract issues and delayed
decisions. This has been mitigated where possible through earlier
than originally planned delivery on other schemes within the
multi-year programme. It should be noted that over half of the
variation (56%) relates to grant funded activity (for example
Levelling Up Fund and Department for Education projects) and the
majority of the former wasn't received until late in the year.
Further details are provided in Appendix 'B'.
 
The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) has
overspent in this year by £79m, with the cumulative DSG
deficit at March 2026 now £102m. This is due to continuing
pressures in Special Educational Needs, which reflects a national
picture across upper tier authorities, with insufficient central
Government grant resources to meet increasing need. Schools outturn
position of schools delegated budget for 2025/26 is an overspend of
£9.195m. This has resulted in the level of school balances
falling to £57.73m. Further details are provided in Appendix
'C'.
 
The Council’s Efficiency Review
continues to play a central role in supporting financial
sustainability and organisational improvement. Phase 1 of the
review informed the 2026/27 budget and Medium-Term Financial
Strategy, with identified savings incorporated into the
Council’s approved financial and transformation plans. The
review is designed as an ongoing programme, with Phase 2 building
on this work to further embed efficiency into business as usual,
identify and deliver further opportunities. An update on progress
to date is provided in Appendix ‘D’.

purpose:
The Edward Stocks Massey Bequest Fund was
established by the will of the late Edward Stocks Massey in 1910,
in order to fund the provision of education (whether mental,
physical, technical or artistic) and the advancements of science,
learning, music or other arts for the inhabitants of
Burnley. 
 
The objectives of the Charity are the
provision of Education (whether mental, physical, technical, or
artistic) and the advancement of science, learning, music or other
arts for the inhabitants of Burnley. Funding for the relief of
rates is not allowed.
 
This year £34,000 has been awarded to
projects, individuals and organisations in the Burnley area. There
are five categories of award:
 

Projects proposed by Lancashire
County Council 
£5,000
Projects proposed by Burnley Borough
Council 
£5,000
Burnley Mechanics
Institute 
£5,000
Individuals and Voluntary
Organisations  
£13,000
University Scholarships for two
students 
£6,000

 
For the first four categories, applications
are first assessed by officers to ensure they meet the criteria and
are then considered by a Joint Advisory Committee made up of three
County Councillors and two Burnley Borough Councillors in the
presence of the Trustees. The Joint Advisory Committee's
recommendations are then presented to the county council for final
approval.

across a number of emerging workstreams, despite increasing demands

content:
The Chairs of the three
Advisory Boards, the Transport Advisory Board, the Economy Advisory
Board, and the Skills Advisory Board, were invited to provide an
update to the meeting on the work their advisory boards had been
undertaken.
 
Councillor Phil Riley provided
an update on the work being undertaken by the Transport Advisory
Board. It was noted that the next Boad meeting had recently been
postponed to July, but work had continued to progress informally,
with ongoing engagement on the Local Transport Plan consultation
for the Implementation Plan. It was highlighted that while some
concerns had been raised by stakeholders, there was a clear
emphasis on the need to begin demonstrating tangible delivery and
visible outcomes. The next meeting of the Board would be held in
July.
 
Councillor Lynn Williams
provided an update on the work being undertaken by the Economy
Advisory Board. It was noted that a meeting of the Board was
scheduled shortly to consider key matters including the Lancashire
Investment Fund and alignment with wider investment opportunities.
The importance of using funding strategically and innovatively to
support the Authority’s growth ambitions was also
emphasised.
 
County Councillor Simon Evans
provided an update on the work being undertaken by the Skills
Advisory Board. It was noted that County Councillor Simon Evans
would no longer be chairing the Advisory Board but would continue
to report the update from the Board to the meeting. Additionally,
there had recently been an extraordinary meeting of the Board to
review the Local Skills Improvement Plan and that preparatory work
for the forthcoming Adult Skills Fund and additional funding for
engineering provision was in progress. Youth unemployment and the
findings of the Milburn Review were also highlighted as a cause of
concern for the Board, and that there was a need for a coordinated
response across partners.
 
The Chair thanked the Chairs of
the Advisory Board's for their updates.
 
Resolved: That the
updates be noted.
topline: The council has decided to note the updates provided by the Chairs of the Transport Advisory Board, Economy Advisory Board, and Skills Advisory Board.

purpose:
This report presents a summary
of the 2025/26 outturn position across the Lancashire Combined
County Authority Revenue and Capital Budgets and summarises the
reserves position. This is the final position for 2025/26 building
upon regular budget monitoring reports previously reported to the
Lancashire Combined County Authority Board.
 
The final revenue outturn for
2025/26 is an underspend of £0.699m, which results in an
increased contribution to reserves in 2026/27. This reflects an
improvement from the position reported at Quarter 3, when an
underspend of £0.056m was forecast. As this has been the
authority’s first annual outturn position, there has
inevitably been fluctuations to previous forecasts, but funds not
spent will result in an increased reserve level that can be
utilised for future investment in priority areas.

purpose:
This
decision is to commence the procurement of a School Meal
Transportation Service for the Authority, which delivers school
meals to a number of school kitchens across the
Authority.
 
The
Authority requires the continued use of a Service Provider to
centrally co-ordinate and manage the transportation of school meals
(hot and cold) in insulated containers from 'production kitchens'
to 'serveries'. At this time of this PIP;
 
There are 37 establishments (18 Production Kitchens and 19
Serveries) actively engaged in this service, which are serviced by
19 set routes per day.
 
The
current contract spend is circa £91,740 per annum.
 
The intention is to
award a contract for an initial term of 2 years with permissible
extension period(s) up to a further 2 years, meaning a potential
contract length of up to 4 years. This would allow for LSRCC to
monitor the contract performance for the initial 2-year term in
order to ascertain the viability of extending the contract with the
awarded service provider.
 
It
is anticipated that the spend will rise due to factors such as
inflation of fuel prices. On this basis, a budget of £100,000
per annum (£400,000 over the potential full four-year
contract term) has been identified as appropriate and agreed
between Lancashire School & Residential Care Catering and
Procurement.

purpose:
As part of a countywide administrative
process, we are revoking historic 30mph "Restricted Road" Speed
Limit Orders (SLOs). These roads already carry a default 30mph
speed limit under national legislation and do not require a
separate SLO.

Purpose of Revocation: This revocation is a procedural step to
remove outdated Speed Limit Orders (SLOs) and restore the roads to
their correct legal status as "restricted roads" under Section 82
of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984. It does not change the
actual speed limit or affect existing signage.

Maintaining obsolete Orders can create legal ambiguity and
enforcement challenges. This revocation ensures consistency and
clarity across Lancashire by clearly distinguishing between roads
governed by default 30mph restrictions and those with imposed 30mph
limits.

Background of Legislation: Under the Road Traffic Regulation Act
1984, a 30mph speed limit can apply in two ways:

• 30mph Speed Limit – imposed via a Speed Limit Order
(SLO), typically used where street lighting is absent or
insufficient.
• 30mph Restricted Road – a default limit that applies
automatically to roads with a system of street lighting (lamps no
more than 200 yards apart), without the need for a Speed Limit
Order to be made.

The main distinction between the two is a 30mph speed limit is an
imposed limit, whereas a 30mph restricted road is a default limit
that automatically applies due to street lighting.

If a different speed limit other than 30 mph is required on a
restricted road, a Speed Limit Order (SLO) must be introduced to
override the default.

Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 08/05/2026 until
05/06/2026 which included advertising in the local press and
notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.

remove outdated Speed Limit Orders (SLOs) and restore the roads to

• 30mph Speed Limit – imposed via a Speed Limit Order

insufficient.

automatically to roads with a system of street lighting (lamps no
more than 200 yards apart), without the need for a Speed Limit
Order to be made.

The main distinction between the two is a 30mph speed limit is an
imposed limit, whereas a 30mph restricted road is a default limit
that automatically applies due to street lighting.

If a different speed limit other than 30 mph is required on a
restricted road, a Speed Limit Order (SLO) must be introduced to
override the default.

suitable location. This will enable buses to align correctly,
safely and more efficiently at the stop and allow for effective
enforcement.

The proposal also includes the construction of a raised boarding
platform ensuring safe boarding and alighting of passengers.

For Bus Stops - Formal consultation was carried out between 10
January-2026 until 13 February-2026 which included frontagers to
the proposed location of the Bus Stop being notified and notices
being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees.

Following formal consultation No Objections were received.
content:

Chorley Borough) (Removal and Introduction of Bus Stop Clearway

procurement process.

Construction of a temporary vehicular access to facilitate
permitted development works, Land to the North of Myles Standish
Way, Heath Charnock, Chorley, PR7 3FT.
content:
A report was presented on an
application for the construction of a temporary vehicular access to
facilitate permitted development works on land to the North of
Myles Standish Way, Heath Charnock, Chorley.

Chorley Borough Council, County Councillor Chris Snow, the Coal
Authority, Lancashire County Council Highways Development Control

received, the details of which were set out in the Committee
report.

presented a Powerpoint presentation

looking east on the existing site frontage and looking
west.

planning permission be granted, subject to the conditions relating to time limits, working
programme, highway matters and site restoration as set out in
Appendix 'A' of the Committee report.

purpose:
The County Council is
considering a proposal to formally close an area of highway known
as Ellen Street, Preston, on the grounds that the highway concerned
is unnecessary for public use. 
 
This is following an
application to the County Council as the local Highway Authority to
request the Authority to make an application to the Court for the
public highway to be stopped up under Section 116 Highways Act
1980.
 
The request has been received
from the proprietor of 31 Garstang Road Preston regarding the area
of highway shown hatched in red on the plan attached at Appendix
1
 
The section of highway lies
between No 31 and Nos 33-39 Garstang Road, Preston.  No 31 is a locksmiths shop and Nos 33-39 is a
private nursery. No 31 has a rear door and rear yard door exiting
onto the area. The nursery school has no direct access onto the
area.
 
The area of highway has a
prohibition of driving traffic regulation order introduced in Sept
1989, with the footway continued across the junction closing off
vehicular access.
 
The area is landscaped in flag
paving with tree pits providing environmental enhancement however
over time the area has failed to be maintained with the small trees
vandalised and removed allowing the area to be overgrown by weeds
and becoming an unsightly feature. The area of highway is therefore
serving little purpose-highway benefit and is considered
unnecessary. Pictures attached at Appendix 2.
 
In the event that any
application to the Court for the stopping up of the highway is
successfully received the existing TRO will need to be rescinded
and the illuminated traffic signs removed. In this respect the
applicant is aware that all the costs associated with the stopping
up application and the accompanying works (rescind the TRO and
removal of the traffic signs) will need to be met by the
applicant.
 
Furthermore, there is an
existing road gully located within the area which will applicant
will be obliged to take over ownership and maintenance.  United Utilities also have apparatus in the area
ie manhole (head of a foul sewer system) and a hydrant, and which
they will continue to have access to under their powers.
 
Initial consultation with
relevant organisations and statutory undertakers
(Feb 2025) has been completed
in line with the council's procedures. No objections have been
received to date.

Waste Material in Lancashire contract.
 
This contract provides
transportation services for a range of waste materials to the
Council's existing disposal facilities. This includes
transportation of waste materials which can be recovered, recycled
or composted such as residual waste, asbestos, green waste, paper
and card, glass, cans, plastics, ferrous metals, mattresses and
inert waste.
 
The
majority of journeys are made
transporting waste materials from the Council's Household Waste
Recycling Centres (HWRCs) to the various suppliers
disposal/recovery/recycling/composting facilities.
 
The current contract is due to
expire 31 March 2027. Under the existing terms and conditions, the
contract has the provision to be extended in 12
month periods up to 31 March 2029. The contract requires the
Council to provide a minimum 9 month notice to the supplier, Fox
Brothers (Leyland) Ltd, if the Council wishes to activate an
extension.
 
This decision relates to the
approval of the activation of the next permitted 12 month extension to the Transportation of Waste
Materials in Lancashire contract. The new end date of the contract
will be 31 March 2028.

content:
It is proposed to make changes to the Cabinet
portfolio responsibilities following the establishment of a new
role of Cabinet Member for Civic Pride and the combining of the
roles of Cabinet Member for Resources, HR and Property and Cabinet
Member for Data, Technology, Customer and Efficiency into a new
role of Cabinet Member for Resources, Property and Efficiency. It
is also proposed to make changes to the Lead Members roles and
postholders.

The Leader of the County
Council approved:
 
(i) 
The revised Cabinet portfolio titles and responsibilities as set
out at Appendix 'A' of the report.
 
(ii) 
The establishment of the role of Lead Member for Resources,
Property and Efficiency and the appointment of County Councillor
Hannah Whalley to that role.
 
(iii) 
The continuation of the role of Lead Member for Health and the
appointment of County Councillor Dr Lorenzo More to that role.
 
(iv) 
The establishment of the role of Lead Member for Education and
Social Care and the appointment of County Councillor Martyn Sutton
to that role.
 
(v) 
The establishment of the role of Lead Member for Growth, Technology
and Efficiency and the appointment of County Councillor Luke Parker
to that role.
 
(vi) 
The continuation of the role of Lead Member for Highways and
Transport and that County Councillor John Clemson continue in that
role.
 
(vii) 
That all other Lead Member roles be disestablished to be replaced
by the Lead Member roles set out in recommendations (ii) to
(vi).
 
This decision be implemented immediately for
the purposes of Standing Order C28(3) as any delay could adversely
affect the execution of the County Council's
responsibilities.  The reason for this
is to ensure the changes are made immediately in advance of the
next Cabinet meeting.
topline: The Leader of the County Council has decided to approve changes to Cabinet portfolio responsibilities and Lead Member roles within the council.

vehicles that are parked causing serious problems with regards to

sightlines, impeding access and egress at junctions and access to

allow buses to safely pull in and out without blocking the road and

obstruction by parked vehicles.

 

The order further removes
restrictions that are no longer required to provide additional
unrestricted parking availability for local residents and
businesses improving the amenities of the area.

 

The proposal also formalises
restrictions that are currently on site and corrects
inconsistencies that have been identified within current Orders.
These proposals will not make any changes to the restrictions or
their extents on site, therefore drivers will not be subject to any
changes as a result of these proposals.

purpose:
The purpose of this proposal is to support the Deardengate public
realm improvement scheme, which proposes to introduce a Restricted
Parking Zone and the facilitation of parking, loading and the
movement of vehicular traffic.
This scheme is primarily an amenity improvement scheme for the
length of Deardengate between Blackburn Road and Bury Road, with
new or amended moving traffic restrictions in nearby areas
pertaining to new bus routes.
In line with the aims and design of this scheme, other alterations
to parking restrictions are also to be proposed in a separate
parking order.
One Way Restriction introductions:
Deardengate, from Blackburn Road to Bank Street
The section of Deardengate between Blackburn Road and Bank Street
has been redesigned to improve pedestrian and cycle movements
through Haslingden town centre. This includes widening the
footways, narrowing the carriageways and providing additional
courtesy pedestrian crossing facilities. This proposal introduces a
new one-way restriction, the effect of which would mean vehicles
are only able to travel north along Deardengate to between
Blackburn Road and Bank Street.
John Street, from Regent Street to Union Street
This proposal introduces a new one-way restriction, the effect of
which would only allow vehicular traffic to travel south-west on
John Street between the junctions of Regent Street and Union Street
to provide a clear pathway for the local bus service which can no
longer use Deardengate in a southbound direction.
Hindle Street
This proposal introduces a new one-way restriction on Hindle
Street. The effect of which would allow vehicular traffic to only
travel in an easterly direction form Deardengate into the car park,
effectively only allowing vehicles leaving the car park to do so
via Bank Street in line with the aims of the scheme.
Bank Street
This proposal introduces a new one-way restriction on Bank Street
from its junction with Deardengate to the Bank Street access road
to the car park. This is to supplement the proposed new one-way
restriction on Deardengate. It prevents the possibility of vehicles
travelling westbound on Bank Street to the point where they meet
the end of the new proposed one-way restriction on Deardengate to
the left and the proposed pedestrianised are to the right, leaving
them nowhere to go.
One Way Restriction revocation:
Union Street, from Blackburn Road to John Street
This proposal revokes the existing one-way restriction on Union
Street between the junctions of Blackburn Road and John Street to
allow Union Street to be traversed in both directions by vehicular
traffic to allow traffic to circulate in the local streets.
Prohibition of Driving introductions:
Deardengate, from Bank Street to Bury Road
The section of Deardengate between Bank Street and Bury Road has
been redesigned to become an almost entirely pedestrianised zone to
create an effective event space for the town centre, with the only
exception being for access to the rear of the limited number of
address points on the west side of Deardengate. This proposal
introduces a Prohibition of Driving Except for Access restriction
to the aforementioned premises.
Ratcliffe Fold, from Bell Street to Deardengate
The proposal introduces a new extended section of Prohibition of
Driving Except for Cycles and Access restriction on Ratcliffe Fold
to begin from its junction with Bell Street and ending at its
junction with Deardengate. This is to facilitate cycle movements in
a southerly direction where cyclists are prohibited along the
northern section of Deardengate between Bank Street and Bury
Road.
Removable bollards are also proposed to be introduced on Ratcliffe
Fold at the junction with Deardengate and immediately east of the
access points to the rear of 9 to 45 Deardengate to prevent
vehicular access along this length of Ratcliffe Fold unless
required access has been prearranged.

Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 20th March-2026 until
17th April-2026 which included advertising in the local press and
notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.

Following formal consultation No Objections were received.

Peter Bell, Highway Regulation Manager, took a decision to
approve Lancashire County Council (Deardengate Area, Haslingden,
Rossendale Borough) (Revocation, Prohibition of Driving and One Way
Traffic) Order 202*

purpose:
As part of a s278 Agreement under the Highways
Act 1980 relating to a new housing development it is proposed to
upgrade the existing bus stops on the B6257 Blackburn Road at
Rawtenstall and Market Street, Edenfield with enforceable clearway
markings and signs, allowing buses to pull in safely and
efficiently at the stop.

The purpose of these proposals are to promote sustainable transport
for all users by including the construction of raised platforms,
allowing safe boarding and alighting of passengers.

The proposals include:

a) The introduction of new bus stop clearway on the south east side
of Blackburn Road, resulting in a 132.5 metre reduction of the
advisory cycle lane. The proposed bus stop clearway is to be
located out of the visibility splays of the new development access
road.

b) Removal of the current bus stop and relocation approximately 20
metres north to a more appropriate location on the north east side
of Blackburn Road

c) Introduction of a new bus stop clearway replacing the existing
bus stop flag on the east side of Market Street

d) The extension of the current bus stop clearway on the west side
of Market Street to a length of 27 metres to allow buses to pull in
safely and efficiently at the stop.

Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 20/03/2026 and
17/04/2026 which included advertising in the local press and
notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.

Following formal consultation No Objections were received.

purpose:
Following concerns raised by the local bus
operator Wyre Council. working in partnership with Lancashire
County Council and the Town Council, have developed proposals aimed
at improving traffic flow. This involves constructing a buildout
near Stoops Weind, designed specifically to discourage
inappropriate parking, and extending the existing No Waiting
Mon-Sat 8am-6pm restriction southwards.

Whilst the implementation of this proposal will result in the
removal of two limited waiting parking spaces and corresponding No
Waiting Thursday 8am-6pm restriction on the east side, the measures
are considered necessary to ensure the safe and efficient movement
of traffic, particularly buses, along High Street

Consultations
Formal consultation was carried out between 29 October 2025 and 26
November 2025 which included advertising in the local press and
notices being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the
consultation documents posted on the council's website.

Following formal consultation No Objections were received.

However, comments were submitted by the Town Council and the local
County Councillor regarding wider traffic and parking issues in the
area. Discussions are ongoing between the officer responsible for
the proposal, the Town Council and the local County Councillor to
identify the most effective long term solution to the issues
raised. The County Councillor has also raised these concerns with
the Traffic and Safety Team, as they fall outside the scope of the
current proposal.

purpose:
The document, Building a better Lancashire:
Moving the dial on our priorities in 2026/27', sets out
Lancashire County Council’s priorities and areas of focus for
the year ahead, building on the 2025–2030 Council Plan and
last year’s Improvement Plan. It explains the current
operating context (including rising demand, financial pressures and
local government reorganisation) and identifies six “Move the
Dial” improvement priorities where concentrated effort will
have the greatest impact. It also outlines the intended outcomes
for residents and how progress will be overseen through governance,
performance reporting and key performance indicators.
 
This
is deemed to be a Key Decision, and the requirements of the
council's Cabinet procedure rules (Standing Order C19) have been
complied with. Compliance with Standing Order C18 was not possible
as the county council's financial outturn position, which has
enabled a recommendation to approve further initial investment of
£5m to enhance the programme of highways maintenance funded
from resources brought forward from 2025/26, was not known at the
time of the publication of the Statutory Notice of Forthcoming
Executive Key Decisions.

purpose:

direction for developing Lancashire’s future Model of Care.

inspection findings and explains how we plan to develop options for
the future of our direct delivery of adult social care services,
including the role of Lancashire’s in-house services, with a
focus on improving people’s experience of care and support.

consultation into the provider redesign business case.

shaped and moulded by co-production sessions, demonstrating how our
residents expect services and support to be delivered, whilst also
meeting our statutory duties and delivering the best services
possible to Lancashire residents.
 
The new Lancashire Adult Social
Care Model of Care will be made available for Cabinet to consider
in the Autumn.

For clarity, and to resolve an

"The function of determining
Executive portfolios sits with the Leader and can be varied from
time to time at the discretion of the Leader. Cabinet Members have
been allocated the following areas of responsibility by the Leader.

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
Following the outcome of the SEND inspection,
published on 12 February 2025, and approval of the Priority Action
Plan (PAP), the DfE issued an improvement notice to Lancashire
County Council on 5 June 2025, in response to the areas for
priority action and improvement highlighted in the report. This
report provides a summary of the key achievements since the
Priority Action Plan was published and any areas where action is
still required.
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills, Paul Turner,
Director of Education and Inclusion, Olly Moores, Volunteer with the Participation and
Co-production Team and Suli Hussian, Participation and
Co-production Worker to the meeting. It was noted that Miranda
Hyman and Michelle Pye, Co-Chairs of the Parent Carer Forum were
also present to support the item. 
 
A presentation was given to the committee and
Officers outlined that improving SEND services had been a core
priority over the past 10 months, with a strong emphasis on
partnership working across education, parent carer groups, and
youth participation. It was noted that this collaborative approach
had strengthened governance and ensured a wider range of voices
were shaping the improvement journey. Positive feedback had been
received from the Department for Education and NHS England,
recognising accelerated progress and improved partnership working,
although it was acknowledged that the improvement journey remained
ongoing and complex, particularly given wider system pressures such
as changes within health partners. It was noted that the county
council may be subject to an Ofsted visit, within 18 months of the
original visit.
 
Members were advised that the council had
continued to operate within a formal SEND improvement framework,
including meeting the requirements of an improvement notice and
delivering a multi-year improvement plan. Governance arrangements
had been strengthened through a number
of partnership boards and groups, supporting oversight of
areas such as performance, commissioning and EHCP quality. Officers
highlighted measurable improvements in EHCP timeliness, with
performance increasing significantly from previously low levels,
alongside a substantial reduction in backlog cases. This had been
supported by increased staffing capacity, significant investment,
the introduction of more localised, place-based teams, and the
development of new systems, including a digital EHCP portal. It was
noted over the past 12 months an additional £5m had been
added to the budget from 2025/26 to help manage the backlog and
timeliness. A further investment of £7m would be added to the
budget from 2026/27.
 
Officers also outlined national SEND reform
requirements, including the development of a three-year SEND reform
plan to be submitted to government. The plan had focused on
reshaping provision, including increasing support within mainstream
settings and refining the use of Education, Health and Care Plans
(EHCPs) for those with the highest level of need. It was noted that
these reforms were linked to potential financial benefits,
including the write-off of a significant proportion of the
council’s high needs funding deficit. However, they
emphasised that delivery of the reforms would require continued
system-wide transformation, sustained investment, and ongoing
partnership commitment to secure long-term improvements.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

Members queried why the SEND reform
plan had not been presented to the committee earlier, officers
explained that the plan had been developed at pace following recent
government requirements and would be shared in draft form for
feedback through the Bite Size Session following the meeting, with
Members encouraged to input into its development. The importance of
feedback was highlighted and officers confirmed they planned to
engage with a wide range of stakeholders at an early stage,
including Lancashire MPs, schools, and nurseries through online
sessions.

 

A Member queried the terminology
“SEND reform plan”; officers clarified that the title
had been set nationally by the Department for Education and was not
locally determined.

 

The committee questioned whether
improvements in EHCP timeliness had impacted quality; officers
advised that quality assurance processes were in place, including
audit cycles, and while quality had improved, some variability
remained as new staff were trained.

 

A Member raised concerns regarding
inconsistent messaging from schools suggesting EHCPs may be
withdrawn; officers confirmed that current legislation remained
unchanged, that the system was still open for applications, and
that no child would lose entitlement unless national law changed.
Further to this Members highlighted concerns about parental anxiety
and lack of clarity regarding future SEND arrangements; officers
agreed there was a communication gap and confirmed that clearer
information and guidance would be developed with the Parent Carer
Forum.

 

The Committee noted concerns about
how children with lower level SEND needs would be supported without
EHCPs; officers explained that future reforms aimed to strengthen
mainstream provision and reduce reliance on EHCPs while maintaining
support.

 

A Member queried how SEND services
would be protected under local government reorganisation; officers
confirmed that that the authority was already working on
footprints, and the SEND reform plans were already thinking about
LGR.

 

The challenges around recruitment
were raised, officers advised there had been strong interest in
roles and that recruitment was progressing well. It was noted that
agency staff would continue to be used where necessary to maintain
capacity.

 

A representative from the Parent
Carer Forum emphasised the importance of communication and how this
was being pushed by the forum. Regarding the quality of EHCPs, it
was noted that numbers were coming down, however parental
confidence in the support systems still needed more work; officers
acknowledged this and confirmed ongoing engagement.

 

Member's raised concerns about
inconsistent messaging from schools; officers acknowledged this as
an issue and confirmed it would be addressed through improved
communications. The Committee agreed that clearer and more
consistent messaging to schools and parents would be
recommended.

 

A Member asked about EHCP quality
grading; officers explained this was based on a formal audit tool
and confirmed that processes were in place to improve quality where
required.

 

Regarding delays in EHCP reviews,
officers acknowledged that review timeliness remained an issue and
confirmed that increased capacity would address this going
forward.

 

Youth participation representatives
highlighted opportunities for schools to engage with youth voice
programmes and encouraged Members to promote this locally.

 
Resolved: That the following
recommendations be shared with the Cabinet Member for Education and
Skills:
 

That, at an appropriate stage,
further updates be brought to the committee on the SEND reform
plan, including next steps following public consultation.

 

That further information be provided
on Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) auditing processes and
the approach used to monitor and improve quality.

 

That communication and messaging in
relation to proposed changes be reviewed by all stakeholders to
ensure clarity and consistency.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improving SEND services and reforming provision for children with special educational needs and disabilities

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
This is a summary of the work the Early years
team do and the latest data on take up, sufficiency and quality of
settings.
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills, and Aby Hardy,
Head of Education Improvement, to the meeting.
 
The report provided an overview of the
Council’s statutory duties in relation to early years
provision and childcare sufficiency, including improving outcomes
for children under five, ensuring sufficient childcare places, and
supporting families to access funded provision. It outlined current
performance against national targets, key challenges including
inequalities in outcomes, and the actions being taken to improve
access, quality, and engagement across the county.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

Member's queried how local
performance on the WellComm screening
tool compared nationally and how uptake could be increased, and
officers advised that the tool was not used universally by all
authorities, but Lancashire had adopted it due to its proven
effectiveness, with ongoing work to learn from other areas and
increase uptake through more targeted engagement with settings not
currently using it.

 

Members raised concerns regarding
Family Hubs and low uptake of early years provision, particularly
for two-year-olds in Hyndburn as well as better engagement with
parents. Officers reported that Family Hub usage and footfall had
increased significantly over the past two years, with further
government funding (Best Start for Life) being used to expand
outreach, parenting support, and home learning engagement measure
being put in place in areas of deprivation such to support
this.

 

The committee raised concerns about
SEND outcomes and sought clarification on how SEND was defined, and
officers advised that the data included all children receiving SEND
support, not just those with EHCPs, noting that many children may
not yet have been assessed on entry to settings. Officers explained
that all settings had access to Inclusion Funding, which had been
distributed more quickly in recent months, could be accessed prior
to an EHCP, and would be further strengthened through an expanded
exceptional funding pot from the Government to enable earlier and
more targeted specialist support.

 

Concerns were raised regarding
inconsistency across providers and it
was queried whether some early years providers were less willing to
support children with SEND, the committee asked if figures were
available showing how many early years settings supported children
with SEND. Officers advised that the SEND White Paper made it clear
that all settings were expected to be inclusive, with additional
government funding, specialist support, and potential capital
investment being made available to encourage consistent provision
across all early years settings. The
Cabinet Member for Education and Skills, County Councillor Matthew
Salter acknowledged concerns about variability in SEND provision
across private settings and confirmed that work was underway to
ensure funding followed the needs of children, including the
introduction of rapid access exceptional funding and potential
capital investment to support inclusive environments. It was
emphasised that early year's providers play a vital role in the
education system, and that wider initiatives, including Family
Hubs, would support earlier identification of SEND needs and
improve access to support.

 

A Member raised concerns about the
proposed approach of targeted support to certain areas and reduced
support elsewhere, noting that visits were already very limited
(typically once annually) and questioned how reduced or targeted
visits aligned with the aim of building stronger relationships and
support. Concerns were also expressed about the potential lack of
oversight and consistency, the perceived reduction in support
across early years, and whether the focus should instead be on
improving the quality and impact of staff activity within settings
rather than targeting specific areas. Officers clarified that there
would be no reduction in staffing, but that resources would be
reallocated towards areas of highest need to maximise impact.
Officers confirmed that work would continue to ensure relationships
were maintained while targeting resources more effectively and
acknowledged this required further clarification to ensure the
approach was clearly understood as targeted rather than reduced
provision overall. It was suggested that this was something that
could be looked at further at a future meeting of the
committee.

 

Members sought clarification on the
council’s new statutory duty in relation to holiday clubs,
including the scope of provision, age ranges, and whether
sufficient resources were available to deliver this, particularly
during periods when staff availability may be reduced. Officers
advised that the duty related to assessing and monitoring
sufficiency across all provision (including school and private
providers), supported by additional staffing and Department for
Education funding, and focused on identifying gaps and encouraging
provision rather than direct delivery. Members also raised concerns
about the lack of provision for secondary-aged children
(11–14), particularly during holidays, and highlighted this
as a key gap. Officers confirmed that this area was currently under
review, with work focused on mapping provision and identifying
opportunities, although the duty remained broad and evolving, and
further detail would be provided. It was agreed thata briefing note
be brought back to the Committee setting out the statutory duties
in relation to holiday clubs and extended childcare, including
current provision, identified gaps (particularly for secondary-aged
children), and proposed next steps.

 

Further concerns were raised
regarding the wording in the report suggesting a potential
reduction in support to some settings and clarification was sought.
Officers acknowledged the concerns raised by Members and indicated
that further detail and clarity could be provided on how support
would be targeted and delivered. Further to this, the Cabinet
Member for Education and Skills agreed that in the first instance,
a briefing note would come back to the committee providing detailed
proposals on the future early years support model, including
rationale, data analysis, and impact assessment.

 

A Member queried how take-up rates
for three- and four-year-old entitlements could exceed 100%, and
officers explained this was due to reliance on Department for
Education estimates, with data lag and cross-boundary movement of
children resulting in discrepancies between expected and actual
numbers.

 

Gaps in Ofsted judgements were
queried and whether this indicated delays or high provider
turnover, and officers clarified that while inspections were
typically on a four-year cycle, delays could occur due to Ofsted
capacity, and this did not indicate a high turnover of providers,
which remained low. It was noted that new providers were assessed
by Ofsted within six months for compliance before receiving a full
graded inspection later.

 

Members queried how low wages in
Lancashire compared to other parts of the country and how the cost
of living locally compared nationally. The relationship between low
wages and the cost-of-service provision was also queried. Whilst
officers did not have this information to hand, it was agreed that
as a recommendation of the committee further information would be
requested on comparative wage levels and the cost of living in
Lancashire versus other regions, including consideration of the
relationship between wages and the cost-of-service provision.

 

Further to earlier concerns raised,
Members noted that the reference to consultants only working in
targeted settings could be interpreted as excluding some settings
from support. Officers clarified that targeted settings referred to
those identified as needing support or those requesting assistance.
It was noted that some settings did not require or wish to receive
support. Due to limited resources and funding arrangements, support
was being prioritised; however, officers confirmed that assistance
would still be provided to any setting that requests it.

 

The committee queried how targeting
support based on locality and deprivation would improve outcomes
for children with SEND, noting that SEND needs were present across
all areas. It was also queried if provision for children with
disabilities, including sufficiency of places and suitability of
hours, was considered. Officers explained that deprivation was used
as an indicator, as many children at this stage had not yet been
formally identified as having SEND, and there was a recognised link
between deprivation and higher levels of SEND need. It was
confirmed that support would also be provided to settings outside
of deprived areas where high SEND needs were identified, and that
SEND sufficiency and provision, including for children with
disabilities, was considered as part of the council’s
approach.

 

A Member suggested that, in
considering future proposals, it would be helpful to examine not
only staffing levels but also how staff were deployed within
settings. They emphasised the importance of understanding what
activities staff are undertaking on site and whether there are
differences in practice across different areas. Officers
acknowledged the point, and it was noted that this could be
explored further in future reporting.

 

The Chair summarised by stating that
in general there was a desire for reports to be brought to the
committee at an earlier stage to enable Members to contribute
meaningfully to their development and direction. Further to the
updates in the report, emphasis was placed on early years provision
and proposed changes to support arrangements, including those
relating to childminders. It was agreed that this area should be
included in the committee’s forward work programme, and that
as part of the recommendations to the Cabinet Member a more
detailed report outlining current provision, planned changes, and
statutory responsibilities would assist Members in their continued
scrutiny role.

 
Resolved: That the following
recommendations be shared with the Cabinet Member for Education and
Skills:
 

That a further report / briefing be
brought back to the committee providing detailed proposals on the
future early years support model, including rationale, data
analysis, and impact assessment.

 

That a briefing be provided on the
statutory duty relating to holiday clubs and extended childcare
provision, including current provision, identified gaps, and
proposed next steps.

 

That further information be provided
on comparative wage levels and cost of living in Lancashire versus
other regions, including consideration of the relationship between
wages and the cost-of-service provision and workforce impacts.

 

That the committee include Early
Years provision and childcare sufficiency within its future work
programme for continued scrutiny.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to make recommendations on improving early years provision and childcare sufficiency in Lancashire.

purpose:
This is a decision taken under the Scheme of
Delegation to Officers, as outlined in section 9.52 to make
consequential amendments to the Constitution to correct an error or
resolve an inconsistency.
content:
Heloise Macandrew,
Director of Law and Governance took a decision to make the following changes to the
Constitution of the county council to correct errors or resolve
inconsistencies:
 
Full Council, section 3.4
– for clarity, add wording "Public Questions, Councillor
Questions and Notices of Motion may only be submitted for Ordinary
meetings"
 
Executive, section 5.22 –
for clarity, add wording "with the following exceptions" before
(i), and then add wording "(ii) Decisions to appoint, dismiss, or
change the responsibilities of Cabinet members, Lead Members and
Champions, which shall be approved by the Leader"
 
Councillors, section 8.3 (i)
– to resolve an inconsistency, amend wording to "Undergo an
Enhanced Disclosure and Barring (DBS) Check if required in
accordance with agreed arrangements"
 
Code of Member Conduct, section
8.36 – to resolve an inconsistency, amend wording to "You
must also have due regard to the council's protocols and policies.
In cases of uncertainty, you should seek advice from the Monitoring
Officer."
 
Officers, section 9.23 –
to resolve an inconsistency, remove the word "Commerce" from the
Chief Financial Officer's job title
 
Officers, section 9.33 –
for clarity and to resolve an inconsistency, to make any and all
consequential changes to the list of Proper Officers following
changes to the council's officer management structure.
 
Scheme of Delegation to
Officers, section 9.42 – to resolve an inconsistency, amend
the job title of the Chief Financial Officer to "Director of
Finance"
 
Scheme of Delegation to
Officer, sections 9.51 – to make any and all amendments for
clarity, and to resolve inconsistencies, in the Scheme of
Delegation to Officers, to align with recent changes to the
council's officer management structure and
responsibilities.
 
Section 10, Standing
Orders
 
Section B – Full Council
Procedural Standing Orders
 
4.2 – for clarity, add
wording "who is not a member of a political group" after "any
political group or member"
 
4.4 – for clarity, amend
wording of final sentence to "each alternative Budget or list of
proposed amendments shall be proposed, seconded,
debated  and voted on as if they were a
single amendment"
 
4.6 – to resolve an
inconsistency, amend the wording "above" to "below"
 
4.9(e) – for clarity, add
wording "and any member who is not a member of a political group"
after "the Administration, or their nominees,"
 
4.9(e) – to resolve an
inconsistency, amend the wording "three" to "five"
 
4.9(f) – for clarity, add
wording "or a member who is not a part of a political group" after
"the Administration"
 
21 – to resolve an
inconsistency and for clarity, amend order of proceedings as
follows:
 
"a) Appoint a person to preside
if the Chair and Vice-Chair are absent;
b) Receive apologies for
absence;
c) Receive any announcements
from the Chair or the Chief Executive;
d) Receive any declarations of
interest from members;
e) Public Question
Time;
f) Councillor Question
Time;
g) Confirm the minutes of the
last meeting(s) of the Full Council;
h) Deal with reports of the
Cabinet, committees and Officers for decision
i) Receive reports  of the Cabinet, committees and Officers for
information
j) Consider Notices of Motion;
and
k) Other business, if any,
specified in the agenda."
 
23.1 – for clarity, add
the following wording "(for the purpose of this Standing Order,
this includes the Annual Meeting)" after "The minutes of each
meeting shall be presented to the next Ordinary Meeting of the Full
Council"
 
29.1 – for clarity, add
the following wording "and questions may not be submitted by
representatives of political parties represented on the council"
after "members of the public".
 
30.7 – for clarity, amend
wording to "In the event that a political group does not submit a
question for a Full Council meeting, the question slot will be
allocated to any additional question(s) submitted on a first come
first served basis, provided the question has been received in
accordance with Standing Order 30.4 above"
 
37.1 for clarity, add wording
"Ordinary" before each instance of "Full Council"
 
Section C – Cabinet and
Cabinet Committees Procedural Standing Orders
 
13.1 – for clarity, amend
wording to "Any Lead Member may, in the absence of any Cabinet
Member, attend Cabinet meetings with the agreement of the Leader of
the Council, and participate fully in discussion on all agenda
items, but cannot vote
 
Financial Rules
 
To resolve an inconsistency,
amend wording to remove references to obsolete officer boards under
2.16, 2.23, 2.26, 2.40 (b) and 2.40 (c) and insert wording to
reflect the relevant strategic officer board.
 
Procurement Rules
 
2.3 – To resolve an
inconsistency, amend wording under 2.3 from "Save for the
exceptions listed at 2.10" to "Save as provided at paragraph
2.10"
 
2.10 – To make a
correction in accordance with legislation, add a new section
2.10.7: "The direct award of any contract not exceeding the
relevant UK Procurement Threshold which would otherwise satisfy one
or more Direct Award justification set out in Schedule 5 of the
Procurement Act 2023."
 
8.1 – To make a
correction in accordance with legislation, update each instance of
£214,904 within the threshold tables to £207,720 to
reflect changes as made in a Procurement Policy Notice issued by
Government in November 2025.
 
Section 4,
Committees
 
4.1 – To resolve an
inconsistency, to amend the Committee Structure Chart to reflect
the recent addition of the Cabinet Working Group for Culture, and
the Efficiency Review Cabinet Member Working Group.
 
4.1 – To resolve an
inconsistency, update the terms of reference for the Standing
Advisory Committee on Religious Education (SACRE) to reflect the
most recent version approved by the committee.
 
4.1 – To resolve an
inconsistency, amend the Conduct Committee Terms of Reference (d)
to include wording "in the absence of the Monitoring Officer or
where it would be inappropriate for the Monitoring Officer to take
such a decision under the Scheme of Delegation to
Officers"

purpose:
Rawtenstall Gyratory System is
to undergo an improvement scheme to reduce congestion and enhance
safety. The scheme included carriageway widening lane confirmation
amendments and traffic signal system upgrades.
 
Currently on the southwestern
section of the gyratory, Bury Road, outside no 22, a bus stop is
present, but it has not been in use for a significant period.
Additionally, it is not foreseen that there will be a requirement
for a bus stop in this location. It is proposed that it will be
removed to accommodate for the proposed Goods Vehicle Loading Only
Bay.
 
At this location occupying no
22 and adjacent property is a carpet store. The properties in
question do not have rear vehicular access and therefore deliveries
and loading take place on the Bury Road on an ad hoc
basis.
 
It is proposed to formalise
this by using a section of the wide footway as a loading bay.
Kerbing will be adjusted and footway strengthened to enable
vehicles undertaking the actions in question to undertake loading
and unloading off the through carriageway. This will ensure the
improved traffic flow envisaged by the scheme will be unhindered
and also the loading operation can be undertaken safely. Therefore,
the appropriate Traffic Order is requested to enable its use solely
for the purpose of loading and unloading.
 
Consultations
 
For Bus Stops - Formal
consultation was carried out between 27th February-2026 until 27th
March-2026 which included frontagers to the proposed location of
the Bus Stop being notified and notices being displayed on site.
Divisional county councillors were consulted along with the
council's usual consultees.
 
Following formal consultation
No Objections were received.

purpose:
The purpose of the proposal is to upgrade the
existing bus stops to quality bus stops. This is to allow the buses
to pull in and out safely and allow effective enforcement. A raised
boarding platform will also be installed to ensure safe boarding
and alighting of passengers.
 
The proposals are being pursued as part of a
s278 Agreement under the Highways Act 1980 as part of a new housing
development on Carrington Road and the bus stop upgrade is being
proposed to promote sustainable transport for all
users. 
 
Consultations
 
Formal consultation was carried out between
14/01/2025 and 11/02/2025 which included frontagers to the proposed location of the Bus Stop
being notified and notices being displayed on site. Divisional
county councillors were consulted along with the council's usual
consultees.
 
Following formal consultation 14 Objections
and 1 Adverse comment was received. With 1 Objection subsequently
withdrawn.
 
Having considered the consultation responses,
the Public Transport Section investigated the objects and
recommended the bus stops at Sandy Lane should remain unchanged and
recommended the upgrade of the east bound bus stop outside
Adlington Primary School and a new west bound bus stop at the Canal
Bridge on Park Road.
 
Following reassessment of the proposal, a
modification was advertised between 04/11/2025 and 02/12/2025 to
relocate the proposed Bus Stops as recommended to a new location.
No objections were received for the modified consultation.
 
As the Bus Stops are now being proposed in a
completely different location to the original proposal that
received 14 objections and 1 Adverse comment these would not be
relevant to the new proposal. However, responses were received from
two of the original objectors, one confirming that they were in
favour of the amended proposal, however still wished to keep their
original objection on record and one confirming that they totally
stand by all the grievances as outlined in their original
objection, as this would have been devastating to all residents
affected.
 
Comments received by two of the original
correspondents in response to the modification, stating that they
wished to maintain their original objections, have been noted.
However, as these objections relate to the originally proposed bus
stop clearway location, they are not considered applicable to the
new location.
The main points and subsequent suggestions
raised by the two remaining objectors are detailed in appendix
E

The purpose of the proposed Bus
Stops Clearways is to support the upgrade of the existing bus stops
to quality bus stops. This is to allow the buses to pull in and out
safely and allow for effective enforcement.
 
A raised boarding platform will
also be installed to ensure safe boarding and alighting of mobility
impaired passengers and ensure the bus stops are fully mobility
compliant.
The proposals are being pursued
as part of a Section 278 agreement under the Highways Act 1980.
These proposals are being funded fully by the developer and are
linked to the new housing development and associated planning
conditions on Rosemount Avenue.
 
Consultations
 
For Bus Stops - Formal
consultation was carried out between 14 January 2026 and 11
February 2026 which was then extended between the 2nd March 2026 and the 30th March 2026 to ensure sufficient coverage in the
area. This included frontagers to the
proposed location of the Bus Stop being notified and notices being
displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were consulted
along with the council's usual consultees.
 
Following formal consultation
and the extension No Objections were received.
 

Peter Bell, Highway Regulation Manager, took a decision to
approve Lancashire County Council (Pilling Lane, Preesall, Wyre Borough) (Bus Stop Clearways) Legal
Reference: LSG4/894.21650/AFR
topline: The Director of Highways and Transport has decided to approve the recommendations for Bus Stops Clearways to upgrade existing bus stops for safety and mobility compliance.

purpose:
The Lancashire Pension Fund,
supported by the Fund's pooling partner "LPPI", have considered
investment of £35m into the Eden North project in Morecambe
by way of a 25 year loan.
 
The project is forecasting
annual investment returns of c. 7%-9%. These are in line with the
target returns for the portfolio.
 
However, as part of the due
diligence on this project, LPPI have identified that the post
development financial risks are higher than would ordinarily be
accepted for such a project.
 
Normally LPPI would expect the
ratio between net revenue (after costs) and debt service (interest
and repayments) to be in the region of 1.5x. Should the project
fail, LPPI would take charge of the asset (on behalf of the Pension
Fund) as collateral so the asset can be sold and used to repay the
debt.
 
In order to support the
project, LPPI have advised that they could accept a lower ratio (as
low as 1.2x). However, LPPI has received independent valuations if
the project were to fail, cease to service the debt and LPPI take
possession of the property. These value the asset at £37m
– leaving a risk to the Fund's investment of £35m. This
valuation also assumes the site continues to operate as a leisure
destination which may prove problematic given the reason for the
default would likely be poor trading conditions.
 
Whilst this project attracts a
greater degree of risk than would ordinarily be accepted, there are
other non-investment benefits for the Fund including economic and
social benefits for the local area including increased jobs and
regeneration as well as local reputational risks of not investing
in the project.
 
It is noted that, whilst this
project would be a sizeable element of the Fund's local investment
intentions, it does represent only c 0.3% of the total Fund's
assets.
 
So, whilst the risk for the
project is large, the risk to the overall Fund is low given the
small proportion of the portfolio that this account for. On the
balance of risk, it is considered that the social and economic
benefits of the project to the local area justify the additional
financial risk to the project.
 
Consequently, and having
consulted with the Director of Finance and the Chair of the Pension
Fund Committee, it is agreed to progress with the £35m
investment into Eden North.
